reports.title: The Largemouth Bass With Some of the Longest-Standing State Records
reports.text:
What are your odds of catching a state-record largemouth bass?
In states such as Georgia, Michigan, and Wisconsin, not great. Those states, plus a few others, all boast state records that have been standing for more than 65 years. Are they the untouchables? Well, it would take one freak of a bass in those states to be reeled into the record books.
Let’s look at some of the oldest state records.
Georgia: 22 Pounds, 4 Ounces; Set in 1932
When George Perry and his friend J.E. Page traveled to the Ocmulgee River on June 2, 1932, they didn’t have giant bass in mind. They were simply trying to catch food for the dinner table.

reports.title: North Carolina’s George cruises to victory at Phoenix Bass Fishing League Regional on the Potomac River
reports.text:
MARBURY, Md. – Boater Andrew George of Poplar Branch, North Carolina, caught a three-day total of 15 bass weighing 47 pounds, 13 ounces, to win the Phoenix Bass Fishing League (BFL) Presented by T-H Marine Regional on the Potomac River. The tournament, hosted by Charles County Government, Dept. of Recreation, Parks and Tourism, concluded Saturday. For his win, George earned a prize package valued at $52,500, including a Phoenix 819 Pro with a 200-horsepower Mercury or Suzuki outboard worth $50,000, and a $2,500 Phoenix MLF Bonus.
The Potomac River event served as the Regional championship for the BFL Buckeye, Michigan, Northeast and Piedmont divisions. The field included the Top 45 boaters…

reports.title: Mississippi’s Ellis ekes out win at Phoenix Bass Fishing League Regional on Lake Eufaula
reports.text:
EUFAULA, Ala. – Boater Clayton Ellis of Saltillo, Mississippi, caught a two-day total of 10 bass weighing 36 pounds, 4 ounces, to win the Phoenix Bass Fishing League (BFL) Presented by T-H Marine Regional on Lake Eufaula. The tournament, hosted by Eufaula Barbour County Chamber of Commerce, concluded Friday. For his win, Ellis won $57,000, including a Phoenix 819 Pro with a 200-horsepower Mercury or Suzuki outboard worth $50,000 and a $7,000 Phoenix MLF Bonus.

reports.title: Fall Crappie 101: It’s Nothing Like Fishing the Other Seasons
reports.text:
Fall is finally here, and it brings an entirely different way to target crappie. Gone are the days of 90-degree heat and a bite you have to work for. Something changes when the first cool front blows through: Crappie go from finicky to aggressive almost overnight. It happens the same way every year, all across the country.
I saw it play out again on my last trip up the Tickfaw River here in Southeast Louisiana. I was idling the main river, watching my side scan in about 20 feet of water, not looking for anything specific. Then I saw it. A brush pile with a shad ball hovering over it. Underneath were 15 blips on the screen.

reports.text:
Following a disappointing end to an underwhelming 2025 season (at least by his standards), Jesse Wiggins called his brother. reports.title: USA Sweeps Gold at 2026 Bass Fishing World Championship
reports.text:
Host Team USA took home the win at the 20th Black Bass Fishing World Championship on Lake Hamilton, Arkansas, completing a dominant performance across three days of fishing. Legendary bass angler Kevin VanDam and teammate three-time Redcrest Champion Dustin Connell captured the individual pair title.
The United States finished atop the team standings (133 pounds, 5 ounces) after three demanding days from October 1 through October 3, holding off silver medalist South Africa (100 pounds) and third-place finisher France (90 pounds, 2 ounces). reports.title: Success Lake fell to 11 percent of capacity, and fishing was hit or miss
reports.text: Bass chased shad in the evenings, and anglers who located boiling fish loaded up using crankbaits, jerkbaits, and topwater lures.

reports.title: The lake fell to 11 percent of capacity, and spotted bass fishing improved
reports.text: The lake fell to 11 percent of capacity, and spotted bass fishing improved. Bass anglers found success with finesse plastics, crankbaits, and jerkbaits. Most of the spotted bass action came from main lake points and submerged rock piles.

reports.title: Fishing was good in the southern aqueduct
reports.text: Fishing was good in the southern aqueduct, as striped bass, largemouth bass, and catfish consistently took various baits. Largemouth bass struck topwater poppers and Spook Jr.'s in baitfish and bone colors at first light and again during the evenings, while wacky-rigged YUM Dingers fished on a jig head successfully fooled bass positioned near inlets and concrete bridge pylons.

reports.title: Angler Measures a Lifetime of Fishing in 218 Bass Weighing Over 10 Pounds
reports.text:
For most bass fishermen, catching a 10-pound bass is a lifetime achievement. But for 80-year-old Larry Walker of Irving, Texas, it’s a number he has hit 218 times. And he isn’t finished yet.
The Most Recent Big Catches
Larry Walker, 80, of Irving, Texas, gives a thumbs up with one of two double-digit bass he caught Sept. 8 while fishing J.B. Thomas with Slaunched Guide Service.
On Sept. 8, the longtime angler added two more double-digit bass to his career tally while fishing the West Texas reservoir J.B. Thomas with Christian Gladfelter and Bella of Slaunched Guide Service.

reports.title: Hit Lake Murray’s brush for fall crappie
reports.text:
Don’t miss the fall crappie bite
A s Lake Murray’s water temperature cools down in October, Capt. Brad Taylor of Taylor Outdoors said the crappie fishing gets cranked up.
“October is a great month because you can catch crappie in a number of ways, really just about any way you want to catch them will work,” he said.
One way Taylor targets them this time of year is by fishing brush in the main river channel.
“Fall is kind of a magical time of year for Lake Murray because the shad start working up the river,” he said. “And the crappie follow the bait. If you can find the bait, which isn’t too difficult using electronics, then you can find the crappie.”

reports.title: High Rock crappie fall fishing report
reports.text:
Find the bait, find the crappie
S hane Walser of Yadkin Lakes Crappie Guides (336-978-3737) loves fishing High Rock Lake in October.
“It’s a great time to fish, for numerous reasons. The weather is ideal, the summer lake crowds are gone, and the crappie really pick up the bite with the falling temperatures,” he said.
Electronics play a big role in his fishing this month.
“I usually scan three or four creeks before I’ll even begin fishing this month,” he said. “And I’m not necessarily looking for crappie, but for balls of baitfish.”

reports.title: Yeopim Creek Fliers with Carolina ALL OUT
reports.text:
Fliers are among the most unique panfish in the Carolinas
T he Carolinas are full of numerous species of panfish, and for their size, they all fight like champs. They’re also very tasty. Fliers, although they are found throughout the southeast, are among the least widely distributed panfish, mostly living in swampy, acidic blackwater creeks with low pH.
Where you’ll find fliers, you can always count on finding other panfish as well. They overlap with crappie, bluegill, redbreast and shellcrackers, among other species.
